1. Concept Overview
docs.text:
Automation is one of the most effective ways to eliminate toil. OCI Resource Manager is Oracle’s managed Terraform-based automation service used to provision, update, and tear down infrastructure in a consistent and repeatable manner.

Resource Manager provides:

  • A managed Terraform execution environment
  • State file storage without manual handling
  • Drift detection
  • Policy enforcement and change tracking
  • Integration with IAM, OCI Logging, Monitoring, and Events

With Resource Manager, both IT engineers and developers can treat infrastructure as code (IaC), gaining reliability, repeatability, and reduced operational overhead.

docs.title: 2. How This Applies to IT Engineers and Developers
IT Engineers
docs.text:
• Provision compute, networks, load balancers, storage using Terraform.
  • Standardize environment creation across teams.
  • Automate deployments for dev/test/prod.
  • Reduce risk of configuration drift.

docs.title: Developers
docs.text:
• Spin up application environments consistently.
  • Manage application-focused infrastructure like functions, API gateways.
  • Submit infra changes through version control workflows.

docs.title: Unified View
docs.text: Manual Operations → Terraform Templates → Resource Manager → Automated Infrastructure

docs.title: 3.1 Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
docs.text:
Infrastructure is managed using text-based configuration files instead of manual clicks.

Benefits:

  • Repeatability
  • Version control
  • Peer review and governance
  • Reduced misconfiguration

docs.title: 3.2 Terraform Basics in Resource Manager
docs.text:
Resource Manager natively supports Terraform:

  • Variables
  • Providers
  • Modules
  • State management
  • Plan & Apply lifecycle

docs.title: 3.3 Resource Manager Components
docs.text:
• Stack → A collection of Terraform configuration files
  • Jobs → Plan, Apply, Destroy operations
  • State File → Stored securely in OCI
  • Outputs → Values generated after execution

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Resource Manager?

  • Maintain auditable state files securely
  • Automate deployments with version control or object storage templates

docs.title: 1.2 Why Terraform for SRE?
docs.text:
Terraform helps SREs ensure:

  • Consistency → same infra across dev/stage/prod
  • Repeatability → no manual configuration drift
  • Speed → create complex infra in minutes

docs.text: This hands-on activity teaches students how to design and verify High Availability (HA) using OCI Load Balancer and multiple backend instance pools. Students deploy the Class Enrollment Web App behind a Load Balancer and validate traffic distribution.

docs.title: 1.1 Fault Domains & Redundancy
docs.text:
OCI Availability Domains (ADs) contain Fault Domains (FDs). A fault domain is an isolated group of hardware.

High availability requires:

  • Deploying instances across multiple FDs
  • Ensuring that if one FD fails, the service remains up

In this lab, you will deploy two compute instances in different fault domains to host identical versions of the Class Enrollment App.

docs.title: 1.2 Load Balancing Patterns
docs.text:
Load balancers improve HA by:

  • Distributing traffic evenly across backend servers
  • Detecting unhealthy instances
  • Automatically routing traffic away from failures

Recommended pattern:

  • Public Load Balancer → Backend Set → Instance Pool with multiple instances

docs.title: 1.3 Stateless Design Principles
docs.text:
Stateless applications:

  • Store no user session data in the instance
  • Use external shared systems (DB, cache, object storage)
  • Allow easy scaling and failover

The Class Enrollment App (Flask + React + SQLite or DB) can be treated as stateless if:

  • Sessions are stored in cookies or DB
  • Compute node does not store critical state

docs.title: 2. Hands-On Task 1 — Deploy App Behind OCI Load Balancer
Purpose: Place your application behind a public Load Balancer for HA.
Steps:
docs.text:
1. Open Navigation Menu (☰) → Networking → Load Balancers.
  2. Click Create Load Balancer.

  3. Choose:

  4. Name: <student-id>-lb

  5. Visibility: Public

  7. Under Networking:

  8. Select your VCN: <student-id>-vcn

  9. Create or select a public subnet
  10. Click Next.

docs.title: Frontend Listener Configuration:
docs.text:
• Listener Name: http-listener

docs.text: A public load balancer is created and ready for backend attachment.

You will:
docs.text:

docs.title: A. Create Instance Configuration
docs.text:

docs.title: Purpose: Confirm that traffic load is balanced across both app servers.

import os
INSTANCE_ID = os.getenv('HOSTNAME', 'unknown')

def home():

docs.text:
This hands-on activity focuses on two core resilience practices:

  1. Storing secrets securely using OCI Vault
  2. Retrieving a secret safely from a Compute instance

These skills are foundational for building secure, fault‑tolerant, and recoverable systems.

docs.title: 1.1 Backups & Snapshots (Why They Matter)
docs.text:
Although not used directly in this lab, understanding them is essential:

  • Backups → long-term copies of block volumes or databases.
  • Snapshots → point‑in‑time captures for fast recovery.

SREs use them for:

  • DR (Disaster Recovery)
  • Rollbacks
  • Protection against corruption & accidental deletion

docs.title: 1.2 Secret Rotation & Secure Configs
docs.text:
Hard‑coding secrets (DB passwords, API keys) is dangerous. Secrets must be:

  • Stored in OCI Vault
  • Accessed securely by applications
  • Rotated without redeploying entire systems
  • Logged and monitored for usage

This lab walks you through securely storing and retrieving secrets.

docs.title: 2. Hands-On Task 1 — Store Secrets in OCI Vault
Purpose: Store an application DB password or API key securely.
A. Create a Vault
docs.text:
1. Open Navigation Menu (☰) → Identity & Security → Vault.
  2. Click Create Vault.

  3. Select:

  4. Type: “Default Vault”

  5. Name: <student-id>-vault
  6. Compartment: your training compartment
  7. Click Create Vault.

docs.title: B. Create a Master Key
docs.text:
1. Inside your vault, open Master Encryption Keys.
  2. Click Create Key.

  3. Enter:

  4. Name: <student-id>-masterkey

  5. Protection Mode: “HSM” or “Software” (either fine for training)
  6. Click Create Key.

docs.title: C. Create the Secret
docs.text:
1. Inside the Vault, open Secrets.
  2. Click Create Secret.

  3. Enter:

  4. Name: <student-id>-db-password

  5. Description: “DB password for Class Enrollment App”
  6. Encryption Key: <student-id>-masterkey
  7. Under Secret Contents, enter a test value such as:

SuperSecretP@ss123
5. Click Create Secret.

docs.title: Expected Result:
docs.text: A new secret created in the Vault with encrypted storage.

docs.title: 3. Hands-On Task 2 — Retrieve a Secret from a Compute Instance
Purpose: Retrieve secret programmatically using instance principal.
docs.text: This is how applications securely access secrets at runtime.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Your instance must:

  • Have dynamic group membership
  • Have an IAM policy allowing secret access

docs.title: A. Create Dynamic Group for Your Instance
docs.text:
1. Go to Identity & Security → Dynamic Groups.
  2. Click Create Dynamic Group.
  3. Name: <student-id>-dg
  4. Rule:

ALL {instance.id = '<your-instance-ocid>'}
5. Save.

docs.title: B. Create IAM Policy to Allow Secret Retrieval
docs.text:
1. Open Identity & Security → Policies.
  2. Select your compartment.

  3. Create Policy:

  4. Name: <student-id>-vault-policy

  5. Statement:

    Allow dynamic-group <student-id>-dg to read secret-bundles in compartment <YOUR-COMPARTMENT>
    4. Save.

docs.title: C. Retrieve Secret from Instance (Hands-On Command)
docs.text:
SSH into your instance:

ssh opc@<instance-public-ip>

Install OCI CLI if not installed:

sudo dnf install -y oci-cli

Retrieve the secret value:

oci secrets secret-bundle get --secret-id <secret-ocid> --query "data."secret-bundle-content".content" --raw-output | base64 --decode

docs.title: Expected Result:
docs.text:
The terminal prints:

SuperSecretP@ss123

(Or whatever value you stored.)

This confirms secure retrieval via OCI Vault, not from environment variables or config files.

docs.title: 4. Summary of This Hands-On
docs.text:
You successfully:

  • Created a secure vault
  • Stored a secret using encryption
  • Configured instance identity
  • Applied IAM policies
  • Retrieved secrets securely from the VM

This workflow is the foundation of secure configuration management.

docs.title: Expected policy:

Allow dynamic-group <student-id>-dg to read secret-bundles in compartment <YOUR-COMPARTMENT>

docs.text:

  • Command runs without errors
  • Base64‑decoded secret matches stored value
  • No plaintext secret stored on VM

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Identity & Access Management (IAM) Structure in OCI.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: This diagram introduces the fundamental security model of our cloud platform (OCI). It shows how Identities (Users, Groups, and even Instances) interact with Resources. The critical bridge between them is Permissions (defined by Policies). Note the “Compartments” box; this is a logical container unique to OCI used to isolate resources. This structure ensures that only authorized entities can access specific compute, database, or network resources.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text: A new developer joins the team. You add them to the “Developers” Group. The Policy says “Developers can manage Instances in the Dev Compartment.” They instantly get access without you touching the servers.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The Service Reliability Hierarchy.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Modeled after Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, this pyramid dictates that you cannot build advanced systems without basic foundations. * Monitoring (Bottom): If you can’t see it, you can’t fix it. * Incident Response: When things break, how do you react? * Postmortem: Learning from failure. * Testing: Preventing failure before production. * Capacity Planning: Ensuring future scale. * Product (Top): Only when the system is reliable can you focus on features.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Understanding where engineering roles overlap and differ.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• DevOps: Focuses heavily on the “Pipeline” (CI/CD), Infrastructure as Code (IaC), and breaking silos between Dev and Ops.
  • SRE (Site Reliability Engineering): Focuses on “Production Health” (SLOs, Error Budgets, Incident Response). Their goal is reliability.
  • Shared Ground: Both use Automation and Collaboration tools to achieve their goals.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text: A DevOps engineer builds the Jenkins pipeline to deploy code. The SRE engineer writes the alert that fires if that deployment causes the CPU to spike to 100%.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Specific responsibilities for Engineering roles.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• SRE: Owns Availability, Reliability, and Capacity Planning.
  • Platform Engineer: Owns the internal tools (Service Orchestration, Containerization) that developers use.
  • DevOps: Owns the release mechanics (CI/CD).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: SRE implementation is a journey, not a switch.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: You don’t become Google overnight. 1. Start with Observability (Metrics/Logs). 2. Establish Incident Response (Runbooks). 3. Begin Retrospectives (Post-mortems). 4. Automate Testing & Release. 5. Finally, master Capacity Planning.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The three types of data needed to understand a system: Logs, Metrics, and Traces.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Logs: “What happened?” (Detailed text events, errors).
  • Metrics: “Is it healthy?” (Numbers, counts, gauges over time).
  • Traces: “Where did it happen?” (The journey of a request across microservices).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: How the pillars interact.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: By analyzing how requests travel (Traces), tracking health (Metrics), and reading events (Logs), we gain full visibility into the system. It allows us to move from “The system is slow” to “The Database query on Shard 4 is slow.”

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The structured “Lifecycle” of handling an outage.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
1. Incident Occurs: The alarm fires.
  2. Immediate Response: “Stop the bleeding.” Fix the issue first; find the root cause later.
  3. Investigation: Deep dive into why it happened.
  4. Documentation: Write the Post-Mortem.
  5. System Improved: Implement fixes to ensure it never happens again.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Shifting from “Who broke it?” to “How do we fix the system?”

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Blame Culture: Uses “You” statements. Focuses on punishment. Result: People hide mistakes.
  • Ownership Culture: Uses “System” statements. Focuses on improvement. Result: People report mistakes early.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text: An intern deletes a production database. * Blame: Fire the intern. * Ownership: Ask “Why did the system allow an intern to delete a database without approval?” and add a safeguard.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Work that makes you feel like a robot.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Toil is defined as work that is Manual, Repetitive, Automatable, and Tactical (devoid of long-term value). If you are SSH-ing into servers to restart them every day, that is Toil.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Where SREs spend their time.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Toil often hides in the inner circles: “Ticket Management” and “Alerts”. The goal of SRE is to move from these inner circles (manual response) to the outer circles (Automation, Drill Down, and Engineering).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The Automation Paradox.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: In theory, automation frees up time. In reality, writing and maintaining the automation script is work in itself. Lesson: Only automate tasks that happen frequently enough to justify the development cost.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: A flowchart for deciding when to automate.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Follow this logic: 1. Is it a frequent ticket? 2. Can the application fix itself? (Self-healing). 3. If not, can SRE scripts fix it? 4. If yes -> Automate. If no -> Document the manual fix.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: It gets expensive to fix problems the longer you wait.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Requirements Phase (1x): Fixing a misunderstanding on a whiteboard is free.
  • Testing Phase (15x): Fixing a bug found by QA takes developer hours.
  • Deployment Phase (100x): Fixing a bug in production means downtime, lost revenue, and angry customers.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The automated delivery chain.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: A robust pipeline includes Unit Tests -> Static Code Analysis -> Deployment to QA -> Functional Tests -> Deployment to Stage. Reliability checks (like Quality Gates) must exist at every step.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Safe Deployment Strategy.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Never deploy to 100% of users at once. 1. Deploy to 10% (Canary). 2. Check metrics (Quality Gate). 3. Scale to 33%. 4. Scale to 100%.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Quick visual definitions. * SLI: What actually happened (94%). * SLO: What we wanted to happen (95%). * SLA: What we promised/penalty (Money back if < 90%).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Operating between “Happy” and “Angry”.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Your internal goal (SLO) must be stricter than your external promise (SLA). The gap between the SLA (99.90%) and the SLO (99.95%) is your safety buffer. If you hit the SLA, you have already failed your customer significantly.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Reliability is not 100%.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Formula: Error Budget = 100% - SLO This budget is an asset. You can “spend” it on risky deployments or experiments. If you don’t spend your error budget, you might be moving too slowly (too conservative).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The exponential cost of “nines”.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Notice the drop. 99.0% allows 432 minutes of downtime/month. 99.99% allows only 4 minutes. Every additional “nine” costs significantly more money and effort.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: How fast are we crashing?

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Formula: Burn Rate = Error Consumed / Error Allowed * Rate = 1 means you are consuming budget exactly as planned. * Rate > 1 means you are burning too fast (Alert!).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Visualizing budget consumption.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: The red line (Rate 10) shows the budget hitting 0% in just 3 days. The blue line (Rate 1) lasts the full 30 days. This helps you visualize urgency.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The negotiation between SREs and Developers.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Left Side (High Reliability): Slow deployments, stable system. Use this when budget is empty.
  • Right Side (Fast Innovation): Rapid deployments, higher risk. Use this when budget is full.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Why Averages Fail.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: The Green line (Mean) looks fine. But the Red line (P99) is far to the right. This means 1% of your users are having a terrible experience (23 seconds latency), even if the “Average” user is fine. SREs must monitor the tail (P99).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Google’s standard for monitoring.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
1. Latency: Time taken to serve a request.
  2. Traffic: Demand on the system (req/sec).
  3. Errors: Rate of requests failing.
  4. Saturation: How “full” is the system (CPU/Memory/Disk).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Outside-in vs. Inside-out views.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Black-box: Tests “Does it work?” Checks symptom. (e.g., Pinging the homepage).
  • White-box: Tests “Why is it breaking?” Checks cause. (e.g., Checking if the Java Heap is full).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The 50/50 Rule.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: An SRE team should spend max 50% of time on “Ops/Toil” (Blue). The remaining 50% MUST be spent on “Projects” (Orange) to improve the system and reduce future toil.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The Cycle of Response.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
1. Preparation (Training)
  2. Detection (Monitoring)
  3. Containment (Isolate the issue)
  4. Recovery (Restore service)
  5. Post-Incident (Learn)

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Defining “Disaster”.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• RPO (Recovery Point Objective): How much data can you afford to lose? (Time since last backup).
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): How much time can you be offline? (Time until system is back up).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Simple Traffic Distribution.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Requests are dealt like a deck of cards: 1 to A, 2 to B, 3 to C. Good for simple setups, bad if one server is faster than others.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: High Availability Design.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Diagram showing a Global Traffic Manager (GTM) distributing traffic between two active Data Centers. Both are reading/writing to DBs with replication. This provides maximum throughput and redundancy.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Stopping a failure from cascading.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Closed: Normal operation. Traffic flows.
  • Open: Error threshold reached. Traffic is blocked to allow the service to recover.
  • Half-Open: Sending a few test requests to see if the service is back online.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Defense in Depth.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: No single layer is perfect (they all have holes). By layering defenses (Prevention, Detection, Mitigation, Emergency Response), we ensure that a threat cannot pass through all holes to cause a major incident.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Limiting the blast radius.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Don’t deploy to everyone at once. Send the new version (Orange) to a small subset of users (the “Canary”). If the Canary dies, only a few users are affected.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) workflow.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• init: Initialize provider.
  • plan: Preview changes (Dry run).
  • apply: Create resources.
  • destroy: Tear down.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Logging Pipeline.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Logstash: Collects and transforms logs.
  • Elasticsearch: Stores and indexes data.
  • Kibana: Visualizes data (Dashboards).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Physical Isolation Hierarchy.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Region: A geographic area (e.g., Ashburn, Mumbai).
  • Availability Domain (AD): Isolated Data Centers within a Region.
  • Fault Domain (FD): Isolated racks/hardware within an AD.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Virtual Cloud Network (VCN).

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Public Subnet: Has Internet Gateway (IGW). Web Servers go here.
  • Private Subnet: No direct internet access. Databases go here.
  • Security: This separation prevents hackers from attacking your database directly.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: High Availability Architectures.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text:
• Active-Passive: One server works, one sleeps (Backup). Cheaper, but failover takes time.
  • Active-Active: Both servers work. If one fails, the other takes the full load instantly. More expensive, harder to sync data.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: The total cost of downtime.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Shows that MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime) is the sum of RTO (System recovery) + WRT (Work Recovery / verifying data).

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Logical Isolation.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Compartments organize resources (like folders on a PC). They can be nested (Parent Compartment -> Child Compartment). Policies are attached to compartments to control access.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: ISA 18.2 Standard.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Managing alarms is a lifecycle, not a one-time setup. It involves Philosophy -> Identification -> Rationalization -> Design -> Implementation -> Operations -> Maintenance -> Audit.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text: Managing Secrets securely.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation
docs.text: Diagram showing how an Application retrieves credentials. Instead of hardcoding passwords, the app talks to OCI Vault, which securely retrieves the Secret, authenticated via IAM.
